To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the paleontological record shows long-term ecological and morphological stasis, (2) this stasis is the result of hierarchical ecosystem organization, and (3) the stability of fossil morphospecics is the result of ecological locking.

the paleontological record demonstrates that ecological and morphological stasis can last for millions of years in response to environmental change, and that the stability of fossil morphospeciess can be explained by the hierarchical organization of the ecosystem.

(i) the fossil record of the lower to middle Paleozoic foreland basin is characterized by long intervals of coordinated faunal and morphological stability that are separated by much more rapid periods of ecological and morphologic change, and (ii) these patterns can be explained in part by a principle of evolutionary stability based on hierarchical ecosystem theory, in which the long-term stability of morphologies is seen as the result of "ecological locking."
In summary, our research is concerned with
the evolution of ecosystems and their constituent organisms over long geological time scales.
the challenge of paleontological stasis and the role of the ecosystem in explaining the evolutionary process on geological time scales.
the evolution and ecology of fossil communities, and we are exploring the application of ecological concepts to the study of evolutionary processes.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
paleoecological and morphological stasis are a consequence of hierarchical constraints imposed by the ecosystem on the evolution of species and higher taxa.
the fossil record of the lower to middle Paleozoic Appalachians is consistent with a model of evolutionary stability that emerges from ecosystem theory.
the fossil record of the lower Paleozoic Appalachian basin shows a high degree of ecological stability over intervals of millions of years that are separated by periods of rapid change.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
paleontological stasis is not a phenomenon that can be explained by evolutionary theory.
ecological processes are responsible for the long-term stability of fossil morphospeciess and that the fossil record is a record of the ecological process.
paleoecological and paleontological patterns are the result of a complex hierarchy of ecological processes, and that the evolutionary record of fossil morphologies reflects this hierarchy.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the paleontological record is a record of ecological processes and that paleontology is a science of ecology.
paleoecology is a fundamental aspect of the evolutionary process, and the fossil record can provide a unique perspective on the nature of evolution.
paleontologists can use hierarchical ecosystem theory to explain coordinated stasis in terms of ecosystem dynamics and to identify the sources of stability that constrain the evolutionary process.
